title: You Told Us Who We Missed
author: Ashlee, RatedEd
summary: RatedEd follows up its earlier series rating professional development providers for teachers by profiling five names that readers said the series had missed. The piece deliberately declines to score these providers, explaining that reader testimony and published work are enough to describe who each person is and whom they would suit, but not enough to put a number on a working consultant. It sorts the five into three consultants to book (Willow Sweeney, Roni Habib, and Leah Mermelstein) and two writers to read (Eric Hudson and Jason Gulya), giving each a background, a description of the work, a fit, and a caution for buyers. The cautions are the most useful part, from the uneasy Top 20 and Bottom 80 labeling in Sweeney's framework to the question of follow-up after a Habib keynote and the surprising structured literacy turn in Mermelstein's current work. The article closes by drawing three patterns across the five: every one of them taught for real, readers surfaced people that marketing did not, and the best recommendations came with concrete specifics.
points: RatedEd treats these five as leads rather than verdicts, refusing to rate consultants whose bookings depend on a score until it can evaluate the work properly.
Willow Sweeney's Top 20 framework is flagged as clarifying for some staffs and uncomfortable for others because it labels people, especially in buildings doing equity work.

Leah Mermelstein, trained in the Teachers College Reading and Writing Project, now leans toward structured literacy and SRSD, so districts that moved to the science of reading should not dismiss her by lineage.
The strongest pattern repeated from the original series: every recommended provider had spent real years in the classroom before training teachers.
Mermelstein's own argument, that workshops paired with ongoing coaching beat either alone, matches the clearest finding across the whole series.
quotes: We rated the first thirty-plus providers after real research into their offerings, evidence, and track records. For these five, we have published work, professional histories, and one reader who has watched Willow Sweeney present twenty times.
So think of this as five leads worth your time rather than five verdicts. When we can properly evaluate the work, we will rate it and say so.

Some educators find that framing clarifying. Others find labeling people uncomfortable, particularly in buildings doing equity work. Neither reaction is wrong, and you should know which one your staff will have before you book it.
As with any keynote, the question to ask is what happens on day two. Ask what follow-up looks like before you sign.
If your district has moved toward the science of reading and you assumed a workshop consultant would not fit, that assumption is worth checking rather than acting on.
Every one of them taught. Not briefly, and not as a credential. Sweeney taught high school social studies.

Readers surface people marketing does not. None of these five came up in our own research for a six-week series. All of them came from educators who had actually sat in the room. That gap between who is visible and who is good is the entire reason we ask.
